```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

```{r install-packages, eval=FALSE}
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "modelr", "broom"))
```

```{r load-packages}
library(tidyverse)
library(modelr)
library(broom)
```

## Task 1: Inspect diamonds

```{r task1}
data("diamonds", package = "ggplot2")

glimpse(diamonds)
summary(diamonds)

# Answers from the output:
# Rows: 53,940
# Columns: 10
# Median price: $2,401
```

## Task 2: Scatter plot with geom_smooth

```{r task2}
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price, colour = cut)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title   = "Diamond price vs carat by cut",
    x       = "Carat (weight)",
    y       = "Price (USD)",
    colour  = "Cut quality"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Interpretation: The fitted lines (one per cut level) all slope upward,
# confirming that heavier diamonds cost more regardless of cut quality.
# The lines are roughly parallel, suggesting the effect of cut is mostly
# an intercept shift — Ideal diamonds command a higher base price
# at any given carat weight, compared to Fair diamonds.
```

## Task 3: Filter with the pipe

```{r task3}
large_diamonds <- diamonds |>
  filter(carat > 2)

nrow(large_diamonds)

# There are 1,655 diamonds with carat > 2 — just over 3% of the full dataset.
```

## Task 4: Summarise by cut

```{r task4}
diamonds |>
  group_by(cut) |>
  summarise(
    mean_price   = mean(price),
    median_price = median(price),
    n            = n()
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_price))

# Counterintuitive finding: 'Fair' cut diamonds have a HIGHER mean price
# than 'Ideal' cut diamonds. This is because cut is confounded with carat —
# Fair-cut diamonds tend to be heavier (more carat) and therefore more
# expensive on raw price. To see the pure effect of cut on price,
# we need to control for carat size. This is exactly what regression does.
```
